title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
description: Brute force to optimized: instant updates but a full re-sum per query on a plain array versus a Fenwick tree balancing both update and sumRange to O(log n).

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Design a class that supports two operations on an integer array: update(index, val), which changes the value at index to val, and sumRange(left, right), which returns the sum of the elements between indices left and right, inclusive. Both operations can be called any number of times, in any order.

blocks.text: Maintain an array that can be updated at a single position at any time, while also answering "what is the sum of this range" queries, both operations needing to be efficient even when called repeatedly and in any interleaved order.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Ledger That Supports Both Editing an Entry and Summing a Range Quickly
blocks.text: Picture a running ledger of daily transactions. A plain running-total (prefix sum) array answers "sum of days i through j" instantly, but editing a single day's entry would force recomputing every running total after it. A Fenwick tree instead organizes the ledger into overlapping partial sums, so both editing a day and summing a range only ever touch a handful of entries.

blocks.caption: A Fenwick tree: every update or query touches only O(log n) nodes

blocks.text: sumRange(0,2) returns 9 (1+3+5). After update(1,2), the array becomes [1,2,5], and sumRange(0,2) now returns 8 (1+2+5).

Before choosing between a plain array (fast update, slow range sum) or a plain prefix sum array (fast range sum, slow update), notice a data structure exists that makes both operations efficient at once.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A plain array supports O(1) updates but O(n) range sums (adding up every element in the range each time).

Observation 2: A plain prefix sum array supports O(1) range sums but O(n) updates (every later prefix sum shifts when one element changes).

Observation 3: A Fenwick tree splits responsibility for each index among O(log n) "partial sum" nodes, so that both updating a value and querying a prefix sum only ever touch O(log n) of those nodes.

Observation 4: A range sum, sumRange(i, j), is then just prefix(j) minus prefix(i minus 1), two O(log n) prefix queries.
This leads to maintaining a Fenwick tree alongside the array: update adjusts the tree by the change in value, and sumRange combines two O(log n) prefix queries.
Keep a plain array. On update, simply overwrite the value. On sumRange, add up every element in the range directly, from scratch.

items: Store nums as a plain array.
update(i, val): set nums[i] to val directly.
sumRange(i, j): loop from i to j, summing every element directly.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: instant updates, but a full re-sum for every range query

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: update is trivially fast, a single array write.
sumRange recomputes the sum of its range from scratch every single time, with no memory of previous queries.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) per update, but O(n) per sumRange in the worst case.
Space: O(n).

Limitation: if sumRange is called far more often than update, or on large ranges, repeatedly re-summing from scratch becomes the bottleneck; a structure that keeps both operations sub-linear is needed.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why a plain array is not enough here: fast updates come at the cost of slow range sums, since nothing about earlier queries is remembered.

Why a plain prefix sum array is not enough either: it flips the tradeoff, sums become instant, but a single update would need to shift every later prefix sum.

What structure balances both: a Fenwick tree, where each index's contribution is split across O(log n) overlapping nodes, so an update only needs to adjust O(log n) of them, and a prefix sum query only needs to combine O(log n) of them.

The core idea: maintain a Fenwick tree; update adjusts it by the DIFFERENCE between the old and new value, and sumRange(i, j) is prefix(j) minus prefix(i minus 1), each an O(log n) operation.

Build a Fenwick tree from the initial array. On update(i, val), compute the delta between val and the current value at i, and add that delta into the Fenwick tree at position i. On sumRange(i, j), compute the prefix sum up to j, minus the prefix sum up to i minus 1, both O(log n) Fenwick tree queries.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","What happens"],"rows":[["sumRange(0,2)","prefix(2) minus prefix(-1) = 9 minus 0 = 9"],["update(1,2)","delta = 2 minus 3 = -1; Fenwick tree adjusted by -1 at index 1"],["sumRange(0,2)","prefix(2) minus prefix(-1) = 8 minus 0 = 8"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: Fenwick tree updates and prefix queries, both O(log n)

blocks.text: The Fenwick tree structure guarantees that both adding a delta at one position and querying a prefix sum only ever touch O(log n) nodes, since each index's value is folded into a logarithmic number of overlapping partial-sum ranges. Updating by the DIFFERENCE between old and new values keeps the tree consistent without needing to rebuild anything, and any range sum reduces to two prefix queries subtracted.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) per update and per sumRange.
Space: O(n) for the Fenwick tree.

blocks.text: Range Sum Query - Mutable is the canonical use case for a Fenwick tree: whenever both point updates and range sum queries need to be fast, and neither can be sacrificed for the other, a Fenwick tree (or equivalently a segment tree) is the standard tool.

blocks.text: Explicitly comparing the two "obvious" data structures, a plain array and a plain prefix sum array, and explaining why each fails one of the two operations, motivates why a Fenwick tree is the right tool before writing any code.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "both update and range sum need to be fast", think: a Fenwick tree (or segment tree), balancing both to O(log n).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs update in O(1) and sumRange in O(n). The optimized Fenwick tree runs both update and sumRange in O(log n). Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree), balancing point updates and range sum queries.
Core Idea: update by the difference between old and new values, and answer a range sum as two prefix queries subtracted, each O(log n).
Time: O(1) update / O(n) sumRange for the brute force, O(log n) for both in the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: neither a plain array nor a plain prefix sum array can make both operations fast at once; a Fenwick tree is built specifically to balance them.
Interview Difficulty: a standard, well-known data structure application once Fenwick trees are familiar.
One line memory trick: Fenwick tree; update by the delta, query as two prefix sums subtracted.
